blocks.body:
Applying $\mathrm{Hom}(-,\mathbb{Z}/2)$ to the injection $2\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$ gives the zero map, which is not surjective: $\mathrm{Hom}$ is left exact but not exact. The groups $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(A,B)$, the right derived functors of $\mathrm{Hom}$ ([[derived-functors]]), measure this failure. Baer introduced Ext for abelian groups in 1934 to classify ways of building a group out of a subgroup and a quotient; Eilenberg and Mac Lane named it in 1942 and used it in topology, where it is the correction term relating cohomology with coefficients to $\mathrm{Hom}(H_n(X),M)$.

This page defines Ext, computes it over $\mathbb{Z}$ and over other rings, gives five readings of the same groups, proves that $\mathrm{Ext}^1$ classifies extensions (Baer sum, Yoneda Ext), develops projective, injective and global dimension through the vanishing of Ext, proves the universal coefficient theorems, and treats the extension problems, Anderson duality and group cohomology that recent papers need. Those papers use Ext in all these forms: vanishing of Ext as a freeness criterion over local rings (Holanda-Miranda-Neto), $\mathrm{Ext}^1$ and Baer sums inside exact structures on persistence modules (Blanchette-Brüstle-Hanson), Yoneda Ext against derived-functor Ext and group cohomology (Tang), and $\mathrm{Ext}^1(-,\mathbb{Z})$ in the Anderson dual of bordism (the Smith fiber sequence paper). It uses [[tor]] for minimal resolutions and Ext-Tor dualities.

blocks.title: Ext: definition and computations
blocks.body: Ext is the right derived functor of Hom, in either variable. Where Tor records lost injectivity of $-\otimes M$, Ext records lost surjectivity of $\mathrm{Hom}(-,M)$ and $\mathrm{Hom}(M,-)$: Quick's lectures start from the map $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/2)\to\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/2)$ induced by $2\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$, which is zero although $2$ is injective.

blocks.title: Ext
blocks.body:
Let $A, B$ be left $R$-modules. Choose a projective resolution $P_\bullet\to A$ and set
$$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(A,B) &= H^n\big(\mathrm{Hom}_R(P_\bullet,B)\big)\\ &= R^n\mathrm{Hom}_R(-,B)(A),\end{aligned}$$
the cohomology of the cochain complex $0\to\mathrm{Hom}(P_0,B)\to\mathrm{Hom}(P_1,B)\to\cdots$. By the balancing theorem of [[derived-functors]], the same groups arise from an injective resolution $B\to I^\bullet$ of the second variable: $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(A,B)\cong H^n(\mathrm{Hom}_R(A,I^\bullet))$, and the right-hand side is $R^n\mathrm{Hom}_R(A,-)(B)$. Thus:

1. $\mathrm{Ext}^0_R(A,B) = \mathrm{Hom}_R(A,B)$, by left exactness of $\mathrm{Hom}(-,B)$.
2. $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(P,B) = 0$ for $n>0$ if $P$ is projective, and $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(A,I) = 0$ for $n>0$ if $I$ is injective.
3. A short exact sequence $0\to A'\to A\to A''\to0$ gives a long exact sequence
$$\begin{aligned}&0\to\mathrm{Hom}(A'',B)\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,B)\to\mathrm{Hom}(A',B){}\\ &\qquad\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(A'',B)\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B){}\\ &\qquad\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(A',B)\to\mathrm{Ext}^2(A'',B)\to\cdots\end{aligned}$$
and a short exact sequence $0\to B'\to B\to B''\to0$ gives
$$\begin{aligned}&0\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,B')\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,B)\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,B''){}\\ &\qquad\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B')\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)\to\cdots.\end{aligned}$$
The first is the long exact sequence of the derived functors of $\mathrm{Hom}(-,B)$; the second is that of $R^\bullet\mathrm{Hom}(A,-)$, transported along the balancing isomorphism.

Over a PID, using a free resolution $0\to F_1\to F_0\to A\to0$, the definition reduces to Quick's: $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,M)$ is the cokernel of $\mathrm{Hom}(F_0,M)\to\mathrm{Hom}(F_1,M)$, and $\mathrm{Ext}^n = 0$ for $n\ge2$.

The same computation works over any commutative ring $R$ for a non-zero-divisor $x\in R$. The free resolution $0\to R\xrightarrow{x}R\to R/xR\to0$ turns $\mathrm{Hom}_R(-,M)$ into the complex $M\xrightarrow{x}M$ in degrees $0,1$, so $\mathrm{Ext}^0_R(R/xR,M) = \{m\in M: xm = 0\}$, $\mathrm{Ext}^1_R(R/xR,M)\cong M/xM$, and $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(R/xR,M) = 0$ for $n\ge2$; this is the mirror image of the computation of $\mathrm{Tor}(R/xR,M)$ on [[tor]].

blocks.title: Ext over the integers
blocks.body:
For abelian groups:

1. $\mathrm{Ext}^n_{\mathbb{Z}}(A,B) = 0$ for $n\ge2$.
2. $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/m,B)\cong B/mB$; in particular $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/m,\mathbb{Z}/n)\cong\mathbb{Z}/\gcd(m,n)$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/n,\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}/n$.
3. $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\bigoplus_iA_i,B)\cong\prod_i\mathrm{Ext}^1(A_i,B)$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,\prod_jB_j)\cong\prod_j\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B_j)$ (Weibel Proposition 3.3.4).
4. If $A$ is finitely generated with torsion subgroup $T(A)$, then $\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}^r$ ($r$ the rank) and $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,\mathbb{Z})\cong T(A)$.
5. If $A$ is a torsion group, $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,\mathbb{Z})\cong A^* = \mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$, the Pontryagin dual (Weibel Example 3.3.3).

1. Every abelian group has a free resolution of length one.

2. The resolution $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{m}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/m\to0$ gives the complex $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},B)\xrightarrow{m}\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},B)$, i.e. $B\xrightarrow{m}B$ in degrees $0, 1$. Its $H^1$ is $B/mB$ (and its $H^0$ is $B[m] = \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/m,B)$, as it should be). For $B = \mathbb{Z}/n$, $B/mB = \mathbb{Z}/(m,n)$.

3. A direct sum of projective resolutions is a projective resolution of the direct sum, and $\mathrm{Hom}(\bigoplus P^{(i)},B) = \prod\mathrm{Hom}(P^{(i)},B)$; cohomology commutes with products. The second statement is the same with $\mathrm{Hom}(P,\prod B_j) = \prod\mathrm{Hom}(P,B_j)$.

4. Write $A\cong\mathbb{Z}^r\oplus\bigoplus_i\mathbb{Z}/a_i$ by the structure theorem. By 3 and 2, $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,\mathbb{Z})\cong\bigoplus\mathbb{Z}/a_i\cong T(A)$, and $\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}^r$ since there are no non-zero maps from a finite group to $\mathbb{Z}$.

5. Use the injective resolution $0\to\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}\to0$: $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,\mathbb{Z})$ is the cokernel of $\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{Q})\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$. A torsion group has no non-zero maps to the torsion-free group $\mathbb{Q}$, so the cokernel is all of $A^*$. For $A = \mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)$ this gives $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty),\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)^*\cong\mathbb{Z}_p$, the $p$-adic integers, an uncountable group: Ext of a countable group into $\mathbb{Z}$ need not be countable.

blocks.title: One Ext group, two resolutions
blocks.body: Compute $\mathrm{Ext}^i_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Z}/n,\mathbb{Z})$ by resolving the first variable, then by resolving the second, and compare the answers.
blocks.solution:
First variable: $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/n\to0$; applying $\mathrm{Hom}(-,\mathbb{Z})$ gives $\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb{Z}$ in degrees $0,1$. So $\mathrm{Ext}^0 = 0$, $\mathrm{Ext}^1 = \mathbb{Z}/n$, and nothing higher.

Second variable: $0\to\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}\to0$; applying $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/n,-)$ gives $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/n,\mathbb{Q})\to\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/n,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$ in degrees $0,1$. The first group is $0$; the second consists of homomorphisms sending $1$ to an element of $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ killed by $n$, i.e. to one of $0,\frac1n,\dots,\frac{n-1}{n}$, so it is $\mathbb{Z}/n$. Again $\mathrm{Ext}^0 = 0$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^1\cong\mathbb{Z}/n$.

The two computations look nothing alike, and the fact that they agree is the balancing theorem of [[derived-functors]]. The Washington note on injectives and Ext treats this check as the first test of the injective-resolution definition.

blocks.title: The base ring matters
blocks.body: Compute $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2)$ for $R = \mathbb{Z}$, $R = \mathbb{Z}/2$ and $R = \mathbb{Z}/4$.
blocks.solution:
Over $\mathbb{Z}$: $\mathbb{Z}/2$ in degrees $0$ and $1$ (by the theorem above, with $m = n = 2$), zero above.

Over $\mathbb{Z}/2$, a field: $\mathbb{Z}/2$ is free, so $\mathrm{Ext}^0 = \mathbb{Z}/2$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^n = 0$ for $n\ge1$.

Over $\mathbb{Z}/4$, use the periodic resolution $\cdots\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}/4\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}/4\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to0$. Now $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}/4}(\mathbb{Z}/4,\mathbb{Z}/2) = \mathbb{Z}/2$ and multiplication by $2$ induces $0$ on it. So the cochain complex is $\mathbb{Z}/2\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb{Z}/2\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb{Z}/2\xrightarrow{0}\cdots$, and $\mathrm{Ext}^n_{\mathbb{Z}/4}(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2) = \mathbb{Z}/2$ for every $n\ge0$.

Same two modules, three rings, three answers. In each case $\mathrm{Ext}^1$ classifies extensions of $\mathbb{Z}/2$ by $\mathbb{Z}/2$ as modules over that ring: over $\mathbb{Z}$ and over $\mathbb{Z}/4$ the non-trivial class is $0\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to\mathbb{Z}/4\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to0$; over $\mathbb{Z}/2$ the group $\mathbb{Z}/4$ is not a module at all, and every extension splits.

blocks.title: Ext detects projectives and injectives
blocks.body:
1. $P$ is projective if and only if $\mathrm{Ext}^1(P,M) = 0$ for all $M$.
2. $I$ is injective if and only if $\mathrm{Ext}^1(M,I) = 0$ for all $M$, if and only if $\mathrm{Ext}^1(R/J,I) = 0$ for every left ideal $J$.

1. If $P$ is projective, $0\to P\to P\to 0$ is a resolution, so the higher Ext vanish. Conversely, let $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ be exact. The long exact sequence in the second variable contains $\mathrm{Hom}(P,B)\to\mathrm{Hom}(P,C)\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(P,A) = 0$, so $\mathrm{Hom}(P,-)$ preserves surjections.

2. The first equivalence is the same argument with the first-variable sequence: $\mathrm{Hom}(B,I)\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,I)\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(C,I) = 0$. For the second, the long exact sequence of $0\to J\to R\to R/J\to0$ gives
$$\begin{aligned}&\mathrm{Hom}(R,I)\to\mathrm{Hom}(J,I)\to{}\\ &\qquad\mathrm{Ext}^1(R/J,I)\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(R,I) = 0,\end{aligned}$$
so $\mathrm{Ext}^1(R/J,I) = 0$ says exactly that every map $J\to I$ extends to $R$; Baer's criterion ([[homological-algebra]]) finishes.

blocks.title: More tools for Ext
blocks.body:
1. Localisation (Weibel Proposition 3.3.10). Let $R$ be commutative Noetherian, $A$ finitely generated and $S$ multiplicative. Then $S^{-1}\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(A,B)\cong\mathrm{Ext}^n_{S^{-1}R}(S^{-1}A,S^{-1}B)$. The point is that $A$ has a resolution by finitely generated free modules, and $\mathrm{Hom}$ out of a finitely generated free (more generally finitely presented) module commutes with localisation. Consequently $\mathrm{Ext}^n(A,B) = 0$ if and only if it vanishes after localising at every maximal ideal, which is why commutative algebra papers such as Holanda-Miranda-Neto work over a Noetherian local ring from the start. Without finite generation the statement fails.
2. Module structure. For commutative $R$, $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(A,B)$ is an $R$-module, killed by $\mathrm{Ann}(A)$ and by $\mathrm{Ann}(B)$.
3. Yoneda product. Splicing exact sequences gives products $\mathrm{Ext}^m(B,C)\times\mathrm{Ext}^n(A,B)\to\mathrm{Ext}^{m+n}(A,C)$; this makes $\mathrm{Ext}^*(A,A)$ a graded ring (Wikipedia, Ext functor). For a polynomial ring over a field $k$, $\mathrm{Ext}^*(k,k)$ is an exterior algebra, the shadow of Koszul duality.
4. Dualities. Papers use several 'dual' functors built from Hom, and they should not be confused: the Pontryagin dual $A^* = \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(A,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$ of Weibel; the $R$-dual $M^* = \mathrm{Hom}_R(M,R)$; the Matlis dual $M^\vee = \mathrm{Hom}_R(M,E(k))$ over a local ring, with $E(k)$ the injective hull of the residue field; and the canonical dual $M^\dagger = \mathrm{Hom}_R(M,\omega_R)$ over a Cohen-Macaulay local ring with canonical module $\omega_R$. Holanda-Miranda-Neto prove dualities of the form $\mathrm{Tor}_j(M,N^\dagger)^\dagger\cong\mathrm{Ext}^j(M,N)$ under vanishing hypotheses, by playing a free resolution of $M$ against an injective resolution of $\omega_R$ in a double complex. The underlying identity is Hom-tensor adjunction, $\mathrm{Hom}(F\otimes N,E)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(F,\mathrm{Hom}(N,E))$, together with the fact that $\mathrm{Hom}(-,E)$ is exact for injective $E$, so it commutes with homology: $H_j(F_\bullet\otimes N)^\vee\cong H^j(\mathrm{Hom}(F_\bullet,N^\vee))$, i.e. $\mathrm{Tor}_j(M,N)^\vee\cong\mathrm{Ext}^j(M,N^\vee)$ for $\vee = \mathrm{Hom}(-,E)$.

blocks.title: Five readings of Ext
blocks.body: $\mathrm{Ext}^n(A,B)$ is one object; the sources present it through five different doors.

items.label: Resolve the first variable
items.body: $H^n(\mathrm{Hom}(P_\bullet,B))$ for a projective resolution of $A$: Ext measures how far $\mathrm{Hom}(-,B)$ is from exact. Over $\mathbb{Z}$, the cokernel of $\mathrm{Hom}(F_0,M)\to\mathrm{Hom}(F_1,M)$ for a two-term free resolution.

items.label: Resolve the second variable
items.body: $H^n(\mathrm{Hom}(A,I^\bullet))$ for an injective resolution of $B$: Ext is the right derived functor of $\mathrm{Hom}(A,-)$. This is the form available in any abelian category with enough injectives; Wikipedia lists sheaf cohomology as Ext in the category of sheaves.

items.label: Classes of extensions
items.body: $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)$ is the group of equivalence classes of short exact sequences $0\to B\to X\to A\to0$ under Baer sum, with the split sequence as zero; $\mathrm{Ext}^n$ is classes of $n$-step exact sequences (Yoneda). This is Baer's original definition and needs no resolutions at all.

items.label: Maps to a shift
items.body: $\mathrm{Ext}^n(A,B) = \mathrm{Hom}_{D(\mathcal{A})}(A,B[n])$ in the derived category: an $n$-extension is a 'morphism of degree $n$', and the Yoneda product is composition. This is the Stacks Project definition; Tang turns to it in his Section 4.

items.label: Homotopy classes
items.body: $\mathrm{Ext}^n(X,A)$ is the set of homotopy classes of maps from $X$ into the $n$-fold delooping $B^nA$, so that higher Ext is $\pi_0$ of a mapping space.

blocks.title: Indexing and shifts for Ext
blocks.body: Sources agree on the mathematics but not on the bookkeeping. Before reading a paper, check these.

rows.text: Topology texts write $\mathrm{Tor}(A,B)$ and $\mathrm{Ext}(A,B)$ for $\mathrm{Tor}_1^{\mathbb{Z}}$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^1_{\mathbb{Z}}$, since the higher groups vanish over $\mathbb{Z}$.

$\mathrm{Ext}^i(X,Y) = \mathrm{Hom}_{D(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y[i])$ is defined for every integer $i$; for objects of $\mathcal{A}$ it vanishes for $i<0$ and is $\mathrm{Hom}$ for $i = 0$. Here $Y[i]$ is $Y$ moved to cohomological degree $-i$.
Writes the shift as a delooping, $A[n]\simeq B^nA$, so that $\mathrm{Ext}^n(X,A)$ is the set of homotopy classes of maps $X\to B^nA$.

blocks.body:
1. Compute $\mathrm{Ext}^1_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Z}/4\oplus\mathbb{Z}/6\oplus\mathbb{Z},\ \mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2)$.
2. Show that $\mathrm{Ext}^1_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{Z})\neq0$. (Use $0\to\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}\to0$ in the second variable, and show that $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{Q})\to\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$ is not onto.)
3. Let $R = k[x]$ and $M = k[x]/(x^2)$. Compute $\mathrm{Ext}^i_R(M,R)$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^i_R(M,M)$.
4. Let $R$ be commutative and $x$ a non-zero-divisor. Show $\mathrm{Ext}^1_R(R/xR,M)\cong M/xM$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^0_R(R/xR,M)\cong\{m: xm = 0\}$.
5. Show that $\mathrm{Ext}^n_{\mathbb{Z}/p^2}(\mathbb{Z}/p,\mathbb{Z}/p)\cong\mathbb{Z}/p$ for all $n\ge0$.

blocks.title: Extensions and Yoneda Ext
blocks.body:
An extension of $A$ by $B$ is a short exact sequence $\xi\colon 0\to B\xrightarrow{i}X\xrightarrow{\pi}A\to0$. Two extensions $\xi,\xi'$ are equivalent if there is a homomorphism $\varphi\colon X\to X'$ with $\varphi i = i'$ and $\pi'\varphi = \pi$; by the five lemma (or the snake lemma; both are on [[homological-algebra]]) such a $\varphi$ is automatically an isomorphism, so this is an equivalence relation. The split extension is $0\to B\to B\oplus A\to A\to0$. Write $E(A,B)$ for the set of equivalence classes. The order of the letters matters, and not every text uses this one; see the conventions table below.

The main theorem identifies $E(A,B)$ with $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)$. The connecting map gives a direct description of the class: applying $\mathrm{Hom}(-,B)$ to $\xi$ yields $\mathrm{Hom}(X,B)\to\mathrm{Hom}(B,B)\xrightarrow{\delta}\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)$, and the class of $\xi$ is $\delta(\mathrm{id}_B)$. The element $\mathrm{id}_B$ lies in the image of $\mathrm{Hom}(X,B)$ exactly when there is a retraction $X\to B$, i.e. when $\xi$ splits; so $\delta(\mathrm{id}_B)$ is the obstruction to splitting, and $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B) = 0$ forces every extension to split (Weibel Lemma 3.4.1). The proof below uses a more hands-on description through a presentation of $A$.

blocks.title: Ext^1 classifies extensions
blocks.body:
Choose an exact sequence $0\to M\xrightarrow{j}P\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}A\to0$ with $P$ projective, so that $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)$ is isomorphic to the cokernel of $j^*\colon\mathrm{Hom}(P,B)\to\mathrm{Hom}(M,B)$ by dimension shifting ([[derived-functors]]). There is a bijection
$$\Theta\colon E(A,B)\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)$$
sending the split extension to $0$. It sends $\xi$ to the class of $\beta = \tau j$, where $\tau\colon P\to X$ is any lift of $\varepsilon$ through $\pi$; its inverse sends the class of $\beta\colon M\to B$ to the pushout extension $0\to B\to X_\beta\to A\to0$, where $X_\beta = (B\oplus P)/\{(\beta(m),-j(m)) : m\in M\}$. Under $\Theta$, the group law of $\mathrm{Ext}^1$ corresponds to the Baer sum of extensions (Weibel Corollary 3.4.5).

blocks.caption: Comparing an extension with a projective presentation of A. A lift tau of epsilon restricts to beta on M; conversely the left square, for a given beta, is a pushout that builds the extension X_beta.
blocks.alt: Two short exact rows: 0 to M to P to A to 0 on top, and 0 to B to X to A to 0 below, with vertical maps beta from M to B, tau from P to X, and the identity on A.

blocks.body:
The cokernel description. The long exact sequence of $\mathrm{Hom}(-,B)$ for $0\to M\to P\to A\to0$ contains
$$\begin{aligned}&\mathrm{Hom}(P,B)\xrightarrow{j^*}\mathrm{Hom}(M,B)\to{}\\ &\qquad\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(P,B) = 0.\end{aligned}$$

$\Theta$ is well defined. A lift $\tau$ exists because $P$ is projective, and $\pi\tau j = \varepsilon j = 0$ shows that $\tau j$ lands in $i(B)$; regard it as $\beta\colon M\to B$. Two lifts differ by a map $P\to X$ with image in $\ker\pi = i(B)$, i.e. by $i\varphi$ with $\varphi\colon P\to B$, and then the two $\beta$'s differ by $\varphi j = j^*\varphi$, which is zero in the cokernel. If $\psi\colon X\to X'$ is an equivalence, $\psi\tau$ is a lift for $\xi'$ with the same restriction to $M$. So $\Theta(\xi)$ depends only on the class of $\xi$. For the split extension, take $\tau(p) = (0,\varepsilon(p))$, so $\beta = 0$.

The pushout is an extension. In $X_\beta$, put $b\mapsto[b,0]$ and $[b,p]\mapsto\varepsilon(p)$. The first is injective: $(b,0) = (\beta(m),-j(m))$ forces $j(m) = 0$, so $m = 0$ and $b = 0$. The second is well defined and onto. If $\varepsilon(p) = 0$ then $p = j(m)$ and $[b,p] = [b+\beta(m),0]$, so the kernel is the image of $B$. If $\beta' = \beta+\varphi j$ for some $\varphi\colon P\to B$, then $[b,p]\mapsto[b-\varphi(p),p]$ is an equivalence $X_\beta\to X_{\beta'}$ (it carries $(\beta(m),-j(m))$ to $(\beta(m)+\varphi j(m),-j(m)) = (\beta'(m),-j(m))$). So $\Psi[\beta] = [X_\beta]$ is a well-defined map $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)\to E(A,B)$.

They are inverse. For $X_\beta$ the map $\tau(p) = [0,p]$ lifts $\varepsilon$, and $\tau j(m) = [0,j(m)] = [\beta(m),0]$, so $\Theta\Psi[\beta] = [\beta]$. Conversely, given $\xi$ with lift $\tau$ and $\beta = \tau j$, the map $B\oplus P\to X$, $(b,p)\mapsto i(b)+\tau(p)$ vanishes on the elements $(\beta(m),-j(m))$ and so induces $X_\beta\to X$, compatible with the maps from $B$ and to $A$. It is therefore an equivalence, and $\Psi\Theta[\xi] = [\xi]$.

The statement about Baer sums is Weibel's Corollary 3.4.5 and is not proved here; Exercise 2 below asks for the key step.

blocks.title: Baer sum and Yoneda Ext
blocks.body:
Baer sum. Given extensions $0\to B\to X\to A\to0$ and $0\to B\to X'\to A\to0$, form the pullback $Y = \{(x,x')\in X\oplus X' : \pi(x) = \pi'(x')\}$, which contains $B\oplus B$, and divide by the anti-diagonal $\{(i(b),-i'(b))\}$. The quotient $X''$ fits into an extension $0\to B\to X''\to A\to0$, the Baer sum. With it, $E(A,B)$ is an abelian group, the split extension is zero, and $\Theta$ is an isomorphism of groups.

Yoneda Ext. A degree $n$ Yoneda extension of $A$ by $B$ is an exact sequence $0\to B\to Z_{n-1}\to\cdots\to Z_0\to A\to0$. Two of them are called equivalent if they are related by the equivalence relation generated by maps of such sequences that are the identity on $A$ and $B$. In any abelian category, the equivalence classes form a group $\mathrm{Ext}^n_{\mathrm{Yon}}(A,B)$, and the Stacks Project shows (its Lemma 13.27.5) that every element of $\mathrm{Ext}^n(A,B) = \mathrm{Hom}_D(A,B[n])$ comes from a Yoneda extension, with equivalent extensions giving equal elements and conversely. So Yoneda Ext agrees with derived-category Ext, and hence with derived-functor Ext when there are enough projectives or injectives. Tang's paper on profinite and solid modules starts from this comparison: it needs to know when Yoneda Ext and derived-functor Ext agree in the categories it studies, and that is where enough projectives or injectives enter.

Splicing a degree $m$ extension of $B$ by $C$ with a degree $n$ extension of $A$ by $B$ at $B$ gives a degree $m+n$ extension of $A$ by $C$; this is the Yoneda product.

blocks.title: Extensions of Z/p by Z/p
blocks.body: Let $p$ be prime. Find all extensions $0\to\mathbb{Z}/p\to X\to\mathbb{Z}/p\to0$ of abelian groups up to equivalence, and compare with the isomorphism types of $X$. (Weibel, Exercise 3.4.1.)
blocks.solution:
$\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/p,\mathbb{Z}/p)\cong\mathbb{Z}/p$, so there are exactly $p$ classes. Use the presentation $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{p}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/p\to0$: here $\mathrm{Hom}(M,B) = \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/p) = \mathbb{Z}/p$, and the image of $j^*$ is $p\cdot\mathbb{Z}/p = 0$. For $\beta_k(1) = k\in\mathbb{Z}/p$ the pushout is
$$X_k = (\mathbb{Z}/p\oplus\mathbb{Z})/\langle(k,-p)\rangle.$$
For $k = 0$ this is $\mathbb{Z}/p\oplus\mathbb{Z}/p$, the split extension. For $k\ne0$ the element $[0,1]$ has $p[0,1] = [k,0]\ne0$ and $p^2[0,1] = [pk,0] = 0$, so it has order $p^2$ and $X_k\cong\mathbb{Z}/p^2$, with $B$ embedded as the subgroup of order $p$ and the quotient map $X_k\to\mathbb{Z}/p$ sending $[0,1]$ to $1$.

So there are $p$ inequivalent extensions but only two isomorphism types of middle group: $(\mathbb{Z}/p)^2$ once, and $\mathbb{Z}/p^2$ for $p-1$ different classes. Concretely, the non-split classes are $0\to\mathbb{Z}/p\xrightarrow{1\mapsto p}\mathbb{Z}/p^2\xrightarrow{\pi_u}\mathbb{Z}/p\to0$ with $\pi_u(1) = u$ for $u\in(\mathbb{Z}/p)^\times$; an equivalence would be an automorphism of $\mathbb{Z}/p^2$ fixing $p$ (so multiplication by some $a\equiv1\bmod p$) and intertwining $\pi_u,\pi_{u'}$, forcing $u = u'$. Note also that a non-split extension cannot have middle group $(\mathbb{Z}/p)^2$: that is a vector space over $\mathbb{F}_p$, in which every subspace has a complement.

blocks.title: Who is extended by whom
blocks.body: For modules the main references agree: the sequence $0\to B\to X\to A\to0$ is an extension of $A$ by $B$, quotient named first, with class in $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)$. The reverse phrasing also occurs, especially for groups, and at least one set of lecture notes mixes the two, so it is safest to read the variance off the exact sequence.

rows.text: An extension of $A$ by $B$ is $0\to B\to X\to A\to0$ (quotient named first), classified by $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)$.
A degree $i$ Yoneda extension of $B$ by $A$ is $0\to A\to Z_{i-1}\to\cdots\to Z_0\to B\to0$, with class in $\mathrm{Ext}^i(B,A)$: again the right-hand end is named first.
An extension of $X$ by $A$ is $0\to A\to P\to X\to0$, classified by $\mathrm{Ext}^1(X,A)$; same order.

$G$ is an extension of $Q$ by $N$ when $1\to N\to G\to Q\to1$ is exact, and $H^2(G,M)$ classifies extensions of $G$ by $M$; but the group extension article notes that the reversed phrasing, 'extension of $N$ by $Q$', is also used by some authors.

Calls $0\to A\to B\to M\to0$ an extension of $M$ by $A$ (quotient first), but then writes the splitting criterion with $\mathrm{Ext}(A,M)$ for these same extensions of $M$ by $A$, and its proof (lifting $\mathrm{id}_M$ to $B\to M$) is really about sequences $0\to M\to B\to A\to0$. With the letters as in his definition, the criterion should read $\mathrm{Ext}(M,A)$; this is the kind of slip the variance check catches.

1. Show directly that two equivalent extensions have isomorphic middle terms, and give an isomorphism $X\cong X'$ of middle terms for two extensions that are not equivalent.
2. Show that the Baer sum of an extension $\xi$ with the split extension is equivalent to $\xi$.
3. Find all extensions of $\mathbb{Z}/2$ by $\mathbb{Z}/4$ (i.e. $0\to\mathbb{Z}/4\to X\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to0$) up to equivalence, and the middle groups that occur.

5. Show that over a field every Yoneda $2$-extension is equivalent to the trivial one, without computing Ext.

blocks.title: Homological dimension
blocks.body:
The projective dimension $\mathrm{pd}_RM$ is the smallest $n$ such that $M$ has a projective resolution of length $n$ ($\infty$ if there is none); $\mathrm{pd}\,M = 0$ means $M$ is projective. The injective dimension $\mathrm{id}_RM$ is defined dually with injective resolutions. The (left) global dimension of $R$ is $\sup_M\mathrm{pd}_RM$. Papers use these as standing hypotheses ('let $M$ have finite projective dimension'), as conclusions, and, in representation theory, as invariants of algebras: Blanchette-Brüstle-Hanson need the global dimension of an exact structure to be finite for their invariants, and relate a relative global dimension of incidence algebras of grids to representation dimension.

Two consequences of the definitions are used constantly. Schanuel's lemma (Stacks Lemma 10.109.1): if $0\to K\to P\to M\to0$ and $0\to L\to P'\to M\to0$ are exact with $P,P'$ projective, then $K\oplus P'\cong L\oplus P$. So syzygies are well defined up to projective summands, and whether the $n$-th syzygy is projective does not depend on the resolution (Stacks Lemmas 10.109.3-10.109.4, Weibel Lemma 4.1.6). And dimension shifting converts a bound on $\mathrm{pd}\,M$ into the vanishing of Ext, as in the next theorem.

blocks.title: Dimension and vanishing of Ext
blocks.body:
Let $n\ge0$.

1. $\mathrm{pd}_RM\le n$ if and only if $\mathrm{Ext}^{n+1}_R(M,N) = 0$ for all $N$, if and only if $\mathrm{Ext}^i_R(M,N) = 0$ for all $i>n$ and all $N$ (Stacks Lemma 10.109.8, Weibel Lemma 4.1.6).
2. $\mathrm{id}_RN\le n$ if and only if $\mathrm{Ext}^{n+1}_R(R/J,N) = 0$ for every left ideal $J$ (by Weibel's Lemma 4.1.11, the Baer form of the injectivity test, applied to a cosyzygy).
3. Consequently the global dimension of $R$ equals $\sup\{\mathrm{pd}_R(R/J)\}$ over left ideals $J$, and also equals $\sup_N\mathrm{id}_RN$ (Weibel's Global Dimension Theorem 4.1.2; Stacks Lemma 10.109.12 for the cyclic modules; Wikipedia, Global dimension).

1. If $M$ has a projective resolution of length $n$, use it to compute Ext: $\mathrm{Hom}(P_i,N) = 0$ for $i>n$, so $\mathrm{Ext}^i = 0$ for $i>n$. Conversely, suppose $\mathrm{Ext}^{n+1}(M,-) = 0$. Take any projective resolution and let $K_{n-1} = \ker(P_{n-1}\to P_{n-2})$ (with $K_{-1} = M$, and $K_{n-1}$ the image of $P_n$). Dimension shifting along $0\to K_i\to P_i\to K_{i-1}\to0$ gives $\mathrm{Ext}^1(K_{n-1},N)\cong\mathrm{Ext}^{n+1}(M,N) = 0$ for all $N$ (for $n = 0$ this is the hypothesis itself). By the theorem that Ext detects projectives, $K_{n-1}$ is projective, and $0\to K_{n-1}\to P_{n-1}\to\cdots\to P_0\to M\to0$ is a projective resolution of length $n$.

2. If $\mathrm{id}\,N\le n$, compute Ext from an injective resolution of length $n$ (allowed by balancing, [[derived-functors]]) to get the vanishing. Conversely, take an injective resolution $0\to N\to I^0\to I^1\to\cdots$ and let $C^{n-1}$ be the image of $I^{n-1}\to I^n$ (with $C^{-1} = N$), so that $0\to N\to I^0\to\cdots\to I^{n-1}\to C^{n-1}\to0$ is exact. Dimension shifting gives $\mathrm{Ext}^1(R/J,C^{n-1})\cong\mathrm{Ext}^{n+1}(R/J,N)$, and by the Baer form of the injectivity test, $C^{n-1}$ is injective exactly when these vanish for all $J$, and then the displayed sequence is an injective resolution of length $n$.

3. If $\mathrm{pd}(R/J)\le n$ for all $J$, then $\mathrm{Ext}^{n+1}(R/J,N) = 0$ for all $J$ and $N$, so $\mathrm{id}\,N\le n$ for every $N$ by 2. Then $\mathrm{Ext}^{n+1}(M,N) = 0$ for all $M,N$ (compute with an injective resolution of $N$ of length $n$), so $\mathrm{pd}\,M\le n$ for every $M$ by 1.

blocks.title: Dimensions of familiar rings
blocks.body: Find the global dimension of a field, of $\mathbb{Z}$, of $\mathbb{Z}/6$ and of $\mathbb{Z}/4$, and the projective dimension of $k$ over $k[x,y]$.
blocks.solution:
A field: every module is free, so the global dimension is $0$. (Global dimension $0$ means every module is projective, i.e. $R$ is semisimple; Wikipedia lists this criterion.)

$\mathbb{Z}$, or any PID that is not a field: every ideal is free, so $\mathrm{pd}(R/J)\le1$, and $\mathbb{Z}/2$ is not projective, so the global dimension is $1$. Rings of global dimension at most $1$ are called hereditary.

$\mathbb{Z}/6\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\times\mathbb{Z}/3$ is a product of fields, hence semisimple: global dimension $0$.

$\mathbb{Z}/4$: the periodic resolution of $\mathbb{Z}/2$ gave $\mathrm{Ext}^n_{\mathbb{Z}/4}(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2) = \mathbb{Z}/2\neq0$ for every $n$, so $\mathrm{pd}\,\mathbb{Z}/2 = \infty$ by part 1 of the theorem, and the global dimension is infinite. This is the simplest example of a local ring that is not regular: by Serre's theorem (quoted from Wikipedia, Global dimension), a commutative Noetherian local ring has finite global dimension exactly when it is regular, and then the global dimension equals the Krull dimension.

$k$ over $k[x,y]$: the Koszul resolution of [[tor]] has length $2$, so $\mathrm{pd}\,k\le2$; and $\mathrm{Ext}^2(k,k)$, computed from it, is $k\ne0$ (the dual complex $k\to k^2\to k$ has zero differentials). So $\mathrm{pd}\,k = 2$, consistent with Weibel's Corollary 4.4.12 for the localisation at $(x,y)$ and with Hilbert's syzygy theorem that $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ has global dimension $n$.

blocks.title: Minimal resolutions over local rings
blocks.body:
Over a Noetherian local ring $(R,\mathfrak{m},k)$, finitely generated projective modules are free (Weibel Proposition 4.3.11; the Stacks Project uses this, as its Lemma 10.78.2, to prove Lemma 10.109.7 on resolutions by finite free modules), and a finitely generated module $M$ has a minimal free resolution: at each step map $R^{b}$ onto the current syzygy with $b$ the minimal number of generators. In a minimal resolution every differential has its matrix entries in $\mathfrak{m}$, so after tensoring with $k$ all differentials vanish. Therefore
$$\mathrm{Tor}_i^R(M,k)\cong k^{\beta_i},\qquad \beta_i = \operatorname{rank}F_i,$$
and the Betti numbers $\beta_i$ do not depend on the minimal resolution. In particular $\mathrm{pd}_RM = \sup\{i:\mathrm{Tor}_i^R(M,k)\neq0\}$ (Weibel Proposition 4.4.11, whose proof uses minimal generators in the same way), and $M$ is free if and only if $\mathrm{Tor}_1^R(M,k) = 0$. Freeness criteria such as those of Holanda-Miranda-Neto conclude that a finitely generated module over a local ring is free from the vanishing of suitable Ext or Tor groups; this is the simplest criterion of that kind.

Depth, maximal Cohen-Macaulay modules, canonical modules and local duality, which the same paper uses alongside these facts, are not covered on this page (see the paper's Section 1 for its conventions).

1. Prove Schanuel's lemma. (Form the pullback of $P\to M\leftarrow P'$.)
2. Show that if $0\to M'\to M\to M''\to0$ is exact then $\mathrm{pd}\,M\le\max(\mathrm{pd}\,M',\mathrm{pd}\,M'')$.
3. Let $R = k[x]/(x^2)$. Show that every finitely generated $R$-module is free or has infinite projective dimension, and compute the Betti numbers of $k$.
4. Show that a ring of global dimension $0$ has every short exact sequence of modules split.
5. Compute the minimal free resolution and Betti numbers of $R/(x^2,xy)$ over $R = k[x,y]$ localised at $(x,y)$.

blocks.title: Universal coefficient theorems and extension problems
blocks.body: For a space $X$, singular homology with coefficients is the homology of $C_\bullet(X)\otimes M$, and cohomology is that of $\mathrm{Hom}(C_\bullet(X),M)$. The chain groups are free abelian, so the question 'how does $H_n(C\otimes M)$ depend on $H_\bullet(C)$?' is purely algebraic, and Tor and Ext answer it. These were the first applications of the two functors, and they are what the [[cohomology]] page will need.

blocks.title: Universal coefficient theorems
blocks.body:
Let $C_\bullet$ be a chain complex of free abelian groups and $M$ an abelian group. There are natural short exact sequences
$$\begin{aligned}&0\to H_n(C)\otimes M\to H_n(C\otimes M){}\\ &\qquad\to\mathrm{Tor}(H_{n-1}(C),M)\to0,\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}&0\to\mathrm{Ext}(H_{n-1}(C),M)\to H^n(\mathrm{Hom}(C,M)){}\\ &\qquad\to\mathrm{Hom}(H_n(C),M)\to0.\end{aligned}$$
Both split, but the splittings are not natural. (Weibel Theorems 3.6.2 and 3.6.5; more generally the first holds over any ring for a complex of flat modules with flat boundaries, as a Künneth theorem, Weibel 3.6.1.)

Write $Z_n = \ker d_n$ and $B_{n-1} = \operatorname{im}d_n\subseteq C_{n-1}$. Both are subgroups of free abelian groups, hence free. The sequence $0\to Z_n\to C_n\xrightarrow{d}B_{n-1}\to0$ is a short exact sequence of complexes if $Z$ and $B$ are given zero differential, and it splits in each degree since $B_{n-1}$ is free. Tensoring with $M$ therefore keeps it exact, and the long exact homology sequence reads
$$\begin{aligned}&\cdots\to B_n\otimes M\xrightarrow{\ \iota_n\otimes1\ }Z_n\otimes M\to{}\\ &\qquad H_n(C\otimes M)\to B_{n-1}\otimes M{}\\ &\qquad\xrightarrow{\ \iota_{n-1}\otimes1\ }Z_{n-1}\otimes M\to\cdots,\end{aligned}$$
where one checks that the connecting map is $\iota\otimes1$ for the inclusion $\iota\colon B\to Z$. This gives
$$\begin{aligned}&0\to\operatorname{coker}(\iota_n\otimes1)\to H_n(C\otimes M){}\\ &\qquad\to\ker(\iota_{n-1}\otimes1)\to0.\end{aligned}$$
Now $0\to B_n\xrightarrow{\iota_n}Z_n\to H_n(C)\to0$ is a free resolution of $H_n(C)$. By right exactness the cokernel of $\iota_n\otimes1$ is $H_n(C)\otimes M$, and by definition of Tor the kernel of $\iota_{n-1}\otimes1$ is $\mathrm{Tor}(H_{n-1}(C),M)$.

Splitting: since $B_{n-1}$ is free, $C_n\cong Z_n\oplus B_{n-1}$; a retraction $C_n\to Z_n$ composed with $Z_n\to H_n(C)$ gives a map from $C\otimes M$ that splits the first sequence. The retraction is a choice, which is why the splitting is not natural.

The cohomology version is the same argument with $\mathrm{Hom}(-,M)$, which also preserves the degreewise split sequences; the cokernel of $\iota^*\colon\mathrm{Hom}(Z_{n-1},M)\to\mathrm{Hom}(B_{n-1},M)$ is $\mathrm{Ext}(H_{n-1}(C),M)$ by definition, and the kernel of $\iota_n^*$ is $\mathrm{Hom}(H_n(C),M)$ by left exactness.

blocks.title: Cohomology of the Klein bottle from its homology
blocks.body: The [[homology]] page computed $H_0(K) = \mathbb{Z}$, $H_1(K) = \mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2$, $H_2(K) = 0$ for the Klein bottle. Find $H^n(K;\mathbb{Z})$, $H_n(K;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ and $H^n(K;\mathbb{Z}/2)$.
blocks.solution:
Integral cohomology, by the second sequence: $H^0 = \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}$. $H^1 = \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z})\oplus\mathrm{Ext}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}$. $H^2 = \mathrm{Hom}(0,\mathbb{Z})\oplus\mathrm{Ext}(\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}/2$. This is Quick's rule $H^n\cong H_n/T_n\oplus T_{n-1}$: torsion moves up one degree.

Mod $2$ homology, by the first: $H_0 = \mathbb{Z}/2$; $H_1 = (\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2)\otimes\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathrm{Tor}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/2) = (\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$; $H_2 = 0\oplus\mathrm{Tor}(\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2) = \mathbb{Z}/2$. Mod $2$ cohomology: $H^0 = \mathbb{Z}/2$, $H^1 = \mathrm{Hom}(H_1,\mathbb{Z}/2)\oplus\mathrm{Ext}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/2) = (\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$, $H^2 = \mathrm{Ext}(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2) = \mathbb{Z}/2$.

So with $\mathbb{Z}/2$ coefficients the Klein bottle has a top class, $H_2(K;\mathbb{Z}/2) = \mathbb{Z}/2$, as every closed surface does mod $2$, and its Betti numbers mod $2$ are $1,2,1$, those of the torus. The direct check: the chain complex from the homology page has $\partial_1 = 0$ and $\partial_2(U) = a+b-c$, $\partial_2(L) = -a+b+c$; mod $2$ both images equal $a+b+c$, so $\partial_2$ has rank $1$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and the dimensions are $1$, $3-1 = 2$, $2-1 = 1$.

blocks.body:
1. Using the homology of $\mathbb{RP}^2$ ($\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Z}/2$, $0$), compute $H^n(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z})$, $H_n(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ and $H^n(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Q})$.
2. Show that if $H_\bullet(C)$ is finitely generated in each degree then $H^n(C;\mathbb{Z})\cong F_n\oplus T_{n-1}$, with $F_n$ the free part of $H_n$ and $T_{n-1}$ the torsion of $H_{n-1}$.
3. Show that a chain map of free complexes inducing isomorphisms on homology induces isomorphisms on cohomology with any coefficients (use naturality and the five lemma).
4. Find a space or a chain complex of free abelian groups for which no splitting of the universal coefficient sequence is natural with respect to all chain maps. (Hint: consider maps between $\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}$ and its shifts.)

blocks.title: Extension problems
blocks.body:
Long exact sequences determine groups only up to extension. If a computation produces $0\to A\to X\to C\to0$ with $A$ and $C$ known, then $X$ is determined by a class in $\mathrm{Ext}^1(C,A)$, and further information is needed to say which. The Smith fiber sequence paper is a good example of how this appears in research: it computes bordism groups from a long exact sequence, and in its Appendix A and in examples such as Example 6.14 it has to decide whether the resulting extensions split, and meets non-split ones.

The smallest instance: from $0\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to X\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to0$ alone one cannot tell $X = \mathbb{Z}/4$ from $X = (\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$, because $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2) = \mathbb{Z}/2$ has two elements. By contrast, if the outer terms have coprime orders, $\mathrm{Ext}^1(C,A) = 0$ and the extension splits: for example $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/3) = \mathbb{Z}/\gcd(2,3) = 0$, so any $X$ in $0\to\mathbb{Z}/3\to X\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to0$ is $\mathbb{Z}/6$. The same paper also uses Anderson duality of spectra; the part of it that is homological algebra, a short exact sequence with an Ext term, is the subject of the next section.

1. Find all abelian groups $X$ that fit into an exact sequence $0\to\mathbb{Z}/4\to X\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to0$, and say which of them arise from more than one class in $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/4)$.
2. Suppose a long exact sequence yields $0\to\mathbb{Z}\to X\to\mathbb{Z}/n\to0$. Which groups $X$ are possible?
3. Show that if $\gcd(|A|,|C|) = 1$ for finite abelian $A$, $C$, then every extension of $C$ by $A$ splits.

blocks.title: Ext into the integers and Anderson duality
blocks.body:
The Smith fiber sequence paper classifies invertible field theories by the Anderson dual of bordism, $I_{\mathbb{Z}}\Omega^\ast_\xi$, and obtains its long exact sequence of invertible field theories by Anderson-dualising the Smith fibre sequence of spectra (its Section 1, Equation (1.6); its footnote 2 refers to its Section 8.2.2 and to Freed-Hopkins for Anderson duality). The spectra are outside this page, but the homological algebra in Anderson duality is one short exact sequence whose outer terms are $\mathrm{Ext}^1(-,\mathbb{Z})$ and $\mathrm{Hom}(-,\mathbb{Z})$. This section derives it, following Stojanoska's account of Anderson duality (Section 2 of her paper on duality for topological modular forms), and then compares it with the form in which Krulewski's thesis states it (Section 2.4.2, which its author says is modified from Section 8.2.2 of the Smith paper).

The input from topology is as follows. Because $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ is an injective abelian group, $X\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{-\ast}X,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$ is a cohomology theory on spectra, represented by the Brown-Comenetz spectrum $I_{\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}}$; likewise $\mathbb{Q}$ gives $I_{\mathbb{Q}}$. The quotient $\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ induces a map $I_{\mathbb{Q}}\to I_{\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}}$, and the Anderson dual $I_{\mathbb{Z}}$ is its fibre (Stojanoska, following Anderson and Hopkins-Singer). Writing $I_{\mathbb{Z}}X$ for maps from $X$ into $I_{\mathbb{Z}}$, and similarly for the others, one has $\pi_tI_{\mathbb{Q}}X = \mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{-t}X,\mathbb{Q})$ and $\pi_tI_{\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}}X = \mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{-t}X,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$, and the fibre sequence $I_{\mathbb{Z}}X\to I_{\mathbb{Q}}X\to I_{\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}}X$ has a long exact sequence of homotopy groups in which $\pi_tI_{\mathbb{Q}}X\to\pi_tI_{\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}}X$ is composition with $\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$. Everything else is algebra.

blocks.title: Hom and Ext into Z, and Anderson's sequence
blocks.body:
1. For every abelian group $A$ the sequence
$$\begin{aligned}&0\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{Z})\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{Q})\xrightarrow{\ \varphi_A\ }{}\\ &\qquad\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,\mathbb{Z})\to0\end{aligned}$$
is exact, where $\varphi_A$ is composition with $\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$.
2. (Stojanoska, Section 2.) For every spectrum $X$ and every integer $t$ there is a short exact sequence
$$\begin{aligned}&0\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(\pi_{-t-1}X,\mathbb{Z})\to\pi_tI_{\mathbb{Z}}X{}\\ &\qquad\to\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{-t}X,\mathbb{Z})\to0.\end{aligned}$$
In terms of $[X,\Sigma^mI_{\mathbb{Z}}] = \pi_{-m}I_{\mathbb{Z}}X$, the group of degree $m$ classes in the cohomology theory $I_{\mathbb{Z}}$, it reads
$$\begin{aligned}&0\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(\pi_{m-1}X,\mathbb{Z})\to[X,\Sigma^mI_{\mathbb{Z}}]{}\\ &\qquad\to\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_mX,\mathbb{Z})\to0,\end{aligned}$$
which with $m = n+2$ is the sequence in Krulewski's Equation (2.4.19), except that Krulewski writes the first term as the torsion subgroup of $\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{n+1}X,\mathbb{C}^\times)$; the two agree when $\pi_{n+1}X$ is finite (see the pitfall below). If $\pi_mX$ is finitely generated, the sequence splits, non-canonically.

1. $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ are divisible, hence injective by Baer's criterion, so $0\to\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}\to0$ is an injective resolution of $\mathbb{Z}$. Applying $\mathrm{Hom}(A,-)$ to it gives the two-term complex $\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{Q})\xrightarrow{\varphi_A}\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$, whose cohomology is $\mathrm{Ext}^0(A,\mathbb{Z}) = \mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{Z})$ in degree $0$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,\mathbb{Z})$ in degree $1$ (Ext may be computed by resolving either variable, by balancing, [[derived-functors]]). That is the claim; this is the computation made for $A = \mathbb{Z}/n$ in the example with two resolutions.

2. The long exact sequence of the fibre sequence contains
$$\begin{aligned}&\pi_{t+1}I_{\mathbb{Q}}X\to\pi_{t+1}I_{\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}}X\to{}\\ &\qquad\pi_tI_{\mathbb{Z}}X\to\pi_tI_{\mathbb{Q}}X\to\pi_tI_{\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}}X,\end{aligned}$$
that is,
$$\begin{aligned}&\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{-t-1}X,\mathbb{Q})\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{-t-1}X,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}){}\\ &\qquad\to\pi_tI_{\mathbb{Z}}X\to\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{-t}X,\mathbb{Q}){}\\ &\qquad\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{-t}X,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}).\end{aligned}$$
By the splicing lemma ([[homological-algebra]]), $\pi_tI_{\mathbb{Z}}X$ is an extension of the kernel of the second $\varphi$ by the cokernel of the first, and by 1 these are $\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{-t}X,\mathbb{Z})$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\pi_{-t-1}X,\mathbb{Z})$. Put $t = -m$ for the second form. If $\pi_mX\cong\mathbb{Z}^r\oplus T$ with $T$ finite, then $\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_mX,\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}^r$ is free; choosing preimages of a basis gives a section, and the choice is what makes the splitting non-canonical.

blocks.title: Spin invertible field theories, algebraically
blocks.body: Krulewski's Theorem 2.4.21 (after Freed-Hopkins and Grady) identifies deformation classes of reflection-positive invertible field theories of dimension $n$ on spin manifolds with $[MTSpin,\Sigma^{n+1}I_{\mathbb{Z}}]$, and the Pontryagin-Thom theorem (Theorem 2.18 of the Smith paper) identifies $\pi_mMTSpin$ with the spin bordism group $\Omega^{Spin}_m$. Taking as given the groups listed in Krulewski's Example 2.2.45, $\Omega^{Spin}_m = \mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2,0,\mathbb{Z},0,0,0,\mathbb{Z}^2$ for $m = 0,\dots,8$, compute these groups for $n = 0,\dots,7$.
blocks.solution:
With $m = n+1$ the sequence reads $0\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(\Omega^{Spin}_n,\mathbb{Z})\to[MTSpin,\Sigma^{n+1}I_{\mathbb{Z}}]\to\mathrm{Hom}(\Omega^{Spin}_{n+1},\mathbb{Z})\to0$, and it splits because the right-hand group is free. Use $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}) = 0$, $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}/2$, $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}) = 0$, $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}^r,\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}^r$.

- $n = 0$: $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z})\oplus\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}) = 0$.
- $n = 1$: $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z})\oplus\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}/2$.
- $n = 2$: $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z})\oplus\mathrm{Hom}(0,\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}/2$.
- $n = 3$: $\mathrm{Ext}^1(0,\mathbb{Z})\oplus\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}$.
- $n = 4,5,6$: $0$.
- $n = 7$: $\mathrm{Ext}^1(0,\mathbb{Z})\oplus\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}^2,\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}^2$.

The pattern is the one of the universal coefficient theorem for cohomology: the torsion of $\Omega_n$ appears in degree $n$, while the free part of $\Omega_{n+1}$ appears one degree lower; so in the group that Krulewski abbreviates as $\mho^n_\xi$ (Notation 2.4.22), indexed by the dimension $n$ of the field theories, the torsion comes from $\Omega_n$ and the free part from $\Omega_{n+1}$. In his Section 2.5.1, where the sequence is used for anomaly theories, he interprets the free quotient through anomaly polynomials (the local anomaly, visible perturbatively) and the torsion subgroup as the topological theories (the global anomaly). The group-theoretic step is only the short exact sequence and its splitting.

blocks.body:
- Krulewski states the first term of the sequence as the torsion subgroup of $\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{m-1}X,\mathbb{C}^\times)$, characters with values in $\mathbb{C}^\times$, where Stojanoska has $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\pi_{m-1}X,\mathbb{Z})$. They agree when $A = \pi_{m-1}X$ is finite: the exponential sequence $0\to\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}^\times\to0$, $z\mapsto e^{2\pi iz}$, is an injective resolution of $\mathbb{Z}$ (both $\mathbb{C}$ and $\mathbb{C}^\times$ are divisible), so $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,\mathbb{Z})$ is the cokernel of $\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{C})\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{C}^\times)$, and for finite $A$ the group $\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{C})$ is $0$ while $\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{C}^\times)$ is finite. In general they differ, already for finitely generated groups with a free part: $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}) = 0$, but the torsion subgroup of $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{C}^\times) = \mathbb{C}^\times$ is the infinite group of all roots of unity. So Krulewski's form is correct when $\pi_{m-1}X$ is finite, as for the bordism groups in his applications that feed this term; to compute in general, use the Ext form.
- $\mathrm{Hom}(-,\mathbb{Z})$ is not exact, so a long exact sequence of bordism groups does not dualise term by term: applied to $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to0$ it gives $0\to0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}$, which is not onto at the end. The Smith paper instead obtains its long exact sequence (1.6) by taking Anderson duals of a fibre sequence of spectra, where the Ext terms are built in. By contrast $\mathrm{Hom}(-,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$ is exact, so Pontryagin duality does turn exact sequences of groups into exact sequences.

1. Let $A = \mathbb{Z}^r\oplus T$ with $T$ finite. Show that the cokernel of $\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{C})\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{C}^\times)$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Hom}(T,\mathbb{C}^\times)$, and hence to $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,\mathbb{Z})$.
2. Suppose $\pi_{m-1}X\cong\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $\pi_mX\cong\mathbb{Z}/3\oplus\mathbb{Z}^2$. Compute $[X,\Sigma^mI_{\mathbb{Z}}]$.
3. Show that if every homotopy group of $X$ is finite, then $\pi_tI_{\mathbb{Z}}X\cong\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{-t-1}X,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$: for such $X$ Anderson duality is Brown-Comenetz duality shifted by one.
4. Prove that $\mathrm{Hom}(-,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$ takes exact sequences of abelian groups to exact sequences, and use the long exact Ext sequence to describe exactly how far $\mathrm{Hom}(-,\mathbb{Z})$ is from doing so on $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$.
5. Using the oriented bordism groups $\Omega^{SO}_m = \mathbb{Z},0,0,0,\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/2,0,0,\mathbb{Z}^2$ ($m = 0,\dots,8$) of Krulewski's Example 2.2.42, compute $[MTSO,\Sigma^{n+1}I_{\mathbb{Z}}]$ for $n = 0,\dots,7$, assuming the Pontryagin-Thom identification $\pi_mMTSO\cong\Omega^{SO}_m$.

blocks.title: Group cohomology as Ext
blocks.body:
A $G$-module is an abelian group with a $G$-action, i.e. a module over the group ring $\mathbb{Z}[G]$ (see [[group-representations]] for the same idea over a field). The trivial module $\mathbb{Z}$ has every $g$ acting as the identity. For any $G$-module $M$,
$$\begin{gathered}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}[G]}(\mathbb{Z},M) = M^G,\\ \mathbb{Z}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}[G]}M = M_G = M/\langle gm-m\rangle,\end{gathered}$$
the invariants and the coinvariants (the second is Arapura's Lemma 5.29). Invariants are left exact and coinvariants right exact, and their derived functors are group cohomology and homology:
$$\begin{gathered}H^n(G,M) = \mathrm{Ext}^n_{\mathbb{Z}[G]}(\mathbb{Z},M),\\ H_n(G,M) = \mathrm{Tor}_n^{\mathbb{Z}[G]}(\mathbb{Z},M).\end{gathered}$$
The low degrees have classical meanings (Wikipedia, Group cohomology; Arapura Theorem 5.31): $H^0 = M^G$; $H^1(G,M)$ is crossed homomorphisms $f(gh) = f(g)+gf(h)$ modulo the principal ones $f(g) = gm-m$, so $H^1(G,M) = \mathrm{Hom}(G,M)$ for trivial action; $H^2(G,M)$ classifies extensions $1\to M\to E\to G\to1$ inducing the given action; and $H_1(G,\mathbb{Z})\cong G/[G,G]$. The same formula with a commutative ring $R$ in place of $\mathbb{Z}$, $H^n(G,A) = \mathrm{Ext}^n_{R[G]}(R,A)$, is the starting point of Tang's comparison of continuous cohomology of profinite groups with its solid analogue, and the Washington note derives it exactly as here, from $M^G = \mathrm{Hom}_{KG}(K,M)$.

blocks.title: Cohomology of a cyclic group
blocks.body: Let $G = C_n = \langle t\rangle$. Using the periodic resolution from the resolutions section of [[homological-algebra]], compute $H^k(C_n,\mathbb{Z})$ and $H_k(C_n,\mathbb{Z})$ for trivial action, and check $H_1(C_n,\mathbb{Z})\cong C_n^{\mathrm{ab}}$.
blocks.solution:
Apply $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}[G]}(-,\mathbb{Z})$ to $\cdots\xrightarrow{N}\mathbb{Z}G\xrightarrow{t-1}\mathbb{Z}G\xrightarrow{N}\mathbb{Z}G\xrightarrow{t-1}\mathbb{Z}G$. Each $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}G}(\mathbb{Z}G,\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}$ (a map is determined by the image of $1$), $t-1$ induces multiplication by $1-1 = 0$ and $N$ induces multiplication by $n$. The cochain complex is
$$\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{n}\cdots$$
in degrees $0,1,2,3,\dots$. Hence $H^0 = \mathbb{Z}$, $H^{\mathrm{odd}} = \ker(n)/0 = 0$, and $H^{2k} = \mathbb{Z}/n$ for $k\ge1$.

For homology apply $\mathbb{Z}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}G}-$; again each term becomes $\mathbb{Z}$ with $t-1\mapsto0$, $N\mapsto n$, giving $\cdots\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb{Z}$ in degrees $\dots,3,2,1,0$. So $H_0 = \mathbb{Z}$, $H_{\mathrm{odd}} = \mathbb{Z}/n$, $H_{2k} = 0$ for $k\ge1$. In particular $H_1(C_n,\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}/n = C_n^{\mathrm{ab}}$, as Arapura's Theorem 5.31 predicts. Also $H^2(C_n,\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}/n$ classifies the extensions $0\to\mathbb{Z}\to E\to C_n\to1$ (all central, since the action is trivial). Two of them are visible at once: the split one, $E = \mathbb{Z}\times C_n$, and $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb{Z}\to C_n\to0$, which does not split because $\mathbb{Z}$ has no element of order $n$.

blocks.body:
1. Compute $H^k(C_n,\mathbb{Z}/n)$ and $H^k(C_2,\mathbb{Z}_-)$, where $\mathbb{Z}_-$ is $\mathbb{Z}$ with the generator acting by $-1$.
2. Show $H_1(G,\mathbb{Z})\cong G^{\mathrm{ab}}$ for any group $G$ by applying $\mathbb{Z}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}G}-$ to $0\to I\to\mathbb{Z}G\to\mathbb{Z}\to0$, where $I$ is the augmentation ideal, and using $I/I^2\cong G^{\mathrm{ab}}$.
3. Show that $H^n(G,M) = 0$ for $n\ge1$ when $G$ is finite and $M = \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Z}G,A)$ is coinduced. (Use the adjunction from the injectives section of [[homological-algebra]].)

1. Let $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ be an exact sequence of finite abelian groups. Using the long exact Ext sequence with $M = \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$, show that $0\to C^*\to B^*\to A^*\to0$ is exact.
2. Let $R$ be commutative Noetherian local with residue field $k$, and $M$ finitely generated. Show that $M$ is free if and only if $\mathrm{Tor}_1^R(M,k) = 0$.
3. Show that $\mathrm{Ext}^1_{\mathbb{Z}}(A,\mathbb{Z}) = 0$ for a finitely generated $A$ if and only if $A$ is free. Is the finite generation hypothesis used in both directions?
4. Let $R = \mathbb{Z}[x]$. Compute $\mathrm{Tor}_i^R(R/(2,x),R/(2,x))$ for all $i$ using a Koszul resolution, and $\mathrm{pd}_R\,R/(2,x)$.
5. Compute $H^n(C_2\times C_2,\mathbb{Z}/2)$ for $n\le2$ from a free resolution of $\mathbb{Z}/2$ over $\mathbb{F}_2[C_2\times C_2]\cong\mathbb{F}_2[x,y]/(x^2,y^2)$.

blocks.title: Reading the papers
blocks.body:
Here is where each paper's prerequisites from this page are treated.

1. Holanda and Miranda-Neto, Cohen-Macaulay Burch rings. Ext of finitely generated modules over a Noetherian local ring (Ext: definition and computations; more tools for Ext), vanishing criteria for freeness (Ext detects projectives and injectives; minimal resolutions over local rings), projective and injective dimension (homological dimension), Hom-tensor adjunction and dualities of the form $\mathrm{Tor}^\vee\cong\mathrm{Ext}(-,(-)^\vee)$ (more tools for Ext). Tor itself is on [[tor]], and the double complexes behind the dualities are on [[derived-functors]]. Not here: depth, its description by $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,-)$, the depth lemma, the Auslander-Buchsbaum formula and maximal Cohen-Macaulay modules, which are left for a planned page on depth and Cohen-Macaulay modules; nor canonical modules, local duality, or the vanishing of $\mathrm{Ext}^{q}(N,\omega_R)$ for $q>0$ and maximal Cohen-Macaulay $N$, which the proof of their Theorem 2.1 quotes from the literature.
2. Blanchette, Brüstle and Hanson, exact structures for persistence modules. Projectives and their characterisation by $\mathrm{Ext}^1$ (Ext detects projectives and injectives), global dimension (homological dimension), extensions, pullbacks, pushouts and Baer sum (extensions and Yoneda Ext). Exact structures and relative Ext are on [[derived-functors]].
3. Tang, profinite and solid cohomology. Ext as a derived functor and as Yoneda Ext, and their agreement (extensions and Yoneda Ext), computing Ext from a projective resolution (Ext: definition and computations), group cohomology as Ext over a group ring (group cohomology as Ext). Not here: condensed and solid mathematics.
4. Debray et al., the Smith fiber sequence. Extension problems (extension problems), and the short exact sequence behind Anderson duality, with middle term $[X,\Sigma^mI_{\mathbb{Z}}]$ between $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\pi_{m-1}X,\mathbb{Z})$ and $\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_mX,\mathbb{Z})$, with the reason a long exact sequence cannot be dualised by $\mathrm{Hom}(-,\mathbb{Z})$ termwise (Ext into the integers and Anderson duality). Not here: spectra, bordism and Thom spectra themselves, which the reader must take from the paper's Section 2.

- $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)$ counts equivalence classes of extensions, not isomorphism types of the middle module. There are $p$ extensions of $\mathbb{Z}/p$ by $\mathbb{Z}/p$ but only two possible middle groups.
- The universal coefficient sequences split, but not naturally. One may not use the splitting to define maps between cohomology groups of different spaces.
- Ext and Tor depend on the ring: $\mathrm{Ext}^1_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2) = \mathbb{Z}/2$, $\mathrm{Ext}^1_{\mathbb{Z}/2}(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2) = 0$, and over $\mathbb{Z}/4$ every $\mathrm{Ext}^n$ is $\mathbb{Z}/2$. Always record the subscript.
- Ext is a right derived functor (Hom is left exact); Tor is a left derived functor ($\otimes$ is right exact). At least one expository source in the dossier, an REU paper, calls Ext 'left-derived'; that is a slip.

- Derived-functor Ext needs enough projectives or enough injectives. Without them, use Yoneda Ext or the derived category; with them, all three agree.
- Localisation commutes with Ext for finitely generated first arguments over Noetherian rings (Weibel 3.3.10), but not in general; $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{Z}) = 0$ while its 'localisation' at $0$ would be $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{Q})\ne0$.
- 'Higher Ext is just diagram chasing' is a common first impression, as the r/math thread shows. The answers there point to Yoneda's $n$-extensions and to the homotopical reading; the conceptual content is that the groups do not depend on the resolution, which is why they can be computed in whichever way is convenient.

Ext is the right derived functor of $\mathrm{Hom}$, so this page builds on [[derived-functors]] and its balancing theorem, and on [[tor]] for minimal resolutions and dualities. [[cohomology]] of spaces uses the universal coefficient theorem proved here. [[galois-cohomology]] is group cohomology $\mathrm{Ext}^n_{\mathbb{Z}[G]}(\mathbb{Z},M)$ for profinite Galois groups, with continuity built in, which is where Tang's paper begins. [[sheaf-cohomology]] is Ext in the category of sheaves, and [[spectral-sequences]] relate Ext groups computed in different ways. Over [[noetherian-rings]], finitely generated modules have resolutions by finitely generated free modules, which is why Ext commutes with [[localization]] and why the minimal resolutions over [[local-rings]] exist.
